interviewQuestions.question: How would you decide whether a new pipeline should be batch, micro-batch, or streaming?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I start from the freshness requirement, defined by a concrete business consequence, not a vibe. I ask: what actually happens if this data arrives an hour late, a minute late, ten seconds late? If the honest answer is "nothing, it's a report someone opens each morning," that's batch, full stop — nightly is fine and anything more sophisticated is wasted effort.

If there's a real consequence — a fraud transaction clears, a live price is wrong — I don't jump straight to continuous streaming either. I check whether micro-batch, a job running every 1-5 minutes, closes the gap. Most "we need real-time" requirements, pressed on this, tolerate a one-minute window fine, and micro-batch keeps the simpler operational model of a batch job: it runs, it finishes, it either succeeded or failed cleanly.

Only when the requirement genuinely can't tolerate even a short window — the fraud-clears-before-you-can-flag-it case — do I reach for continuous, event-by-event streaming, because that's when its operational cost (offset management, backpressure, exactly-once semantics, an on-call rotation that understands consumer lag) is actually justified by the business need.

The framework in one line: default to batch, upgrade to micro-batch if there's a real but moderate latency need, and justify continuous streaming with a named, specific consequence — never with "real-time is better."

**Testing:** whether you reach for complexity by requirement or by reflex.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: What's the actual operational cost difference between a nightly batch job and a Kafka-based streaming pipeline, beyond just the tooling?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The tooling difference is the visible part; the bigger difference is the failure model. A batch job fails safe — if it errors at 2am, you retry it, the blast radius is one late dashboard, and the fix is usually "re-run the job." A streaming pipeline has to handle failure while data keeps arriving: a consumer crashing mid-stream needs precise offset tracking to avoid dropping or duplicating events, backpressure has to be handled when a downstream sink can't keep up, and any windowed aggregation needs its state checkpointed and correctly recovered after a restart.

Concretely, debugging a stuck batch job usually means reading one log and re-running a command. Debugging a lagging Kafka consumer group means understanding partition assignment, rebalancing behavior, and whether lag is growing because of a slow consumer or a genuine traffic spike — a meaningfully different and deeper skill set that most teams don't have until they've been burned by it once.

That translates into a real staffing cost: a streaming system needs an on-call rotation comfortable with that skill set, ideally more than one person so it's not a single point of failure when that person is on vacation. I've seen teams adopt streaming for the latency win and only discover the staffing cost six months later, when the person who understood the consumer group configuration left.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate operational cost concretely, not just say "streaming is more complex."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Operational cost

interviewQuestions.question: Your team wants to build a real-time streaming pipeline for a use case that, on inspection, doesn't seem to need sub-minute latency. How would you push back constructively?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't push back with "streaming is bad" — I'd push back with a specific question: what decision or action changes because this data is 30 seconds old instead of 6 hours old? If nobody's workflow actually changes — the dashboard is checked once a day regardless of how fresh it is — then the latency reduction has no realized value, and I'd say that plainly.

I'd frame the alternative concretely rather than just saying no: propose micro-batch as a middle path first — a job every few minutes gets you a dashboard that feels current to a human, at a fraction of the build and ongoing operational cost of Kafka plus a stream processor. If that satisfies the actual need, we've avoided taking on offset management, backpressure handling, and a new on-call skill set for zero measurable business benefit.

If the team insists there's a real reason, I'd ask them to name it explicitly and check it against a concrete number — "the sales team needs same-hour visibility into a live promotion" is a real, checkable requirement; "it would feel more modern" is not. I'd rather have that conversation up front than debug consumer rebalancing at 1am six months later for a use case that turned out not to need it.

Ultimately I'd let the requirement decide, and be genuinely willing to build streaming if the requirement holds up under that scrutiny — the goal is rigor, not reflexive conservatism either.

**Testing:** whether you can challenge a technical decision constructively with a concrete alternative, not just gatekeep.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Communication

interviewQuestions.question: You're designing fraud detection for a payments platform. Walk through why this specifically justifies streaming, and what breaks if you get the latency wrong in either direction.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Fraud detection is the canonical case where streaming's cost is justified because the failure mode of batch is structural, not just slow. If scoring runs as a nightly batch job, by the time a transaction is flagged, the funds have already moved — a faster batch schedule doesn't fix this, because the decision window (before the transaction clears) has already closed regardless of how quickly the analysis eventually runs. That's different from a dashboard being stale; there, faster batch scheduling genuinely helps. Here, only scoring within the transaction's own processing window helps at all.

Concretely, I'd design this as a stream processor (Flink or similar) consuming the transaction event stream, scoring each transaction against a fraud model within roughly 100-300ms, and returning a decision before the payment authorization completes — decline, allow, or flag for step-up verification.

What breaks if I get this wrong in either direction: too slow, and legitimate transactions start timing out or getting declined by default because the score didn't arrive in time — a false-decline problem that costs revenue and frustrates real customers. Too aggressive on latency without enough model confidence, and you either under-score (missed fraud, direct financial loss) or over-score (blocking legitimate transactions, which is its own costly failure).

The operational bar this demands — sub-second, highly available, correctly handling backpressure without silently dropping transactions — is exactly the case streaming's cost is built for, unlike most "real-time" dashboard requests that don't carry this severity.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about latency trade-offs with real failure-mode consequences on both sides, not just "faster is better."
